title.en: Cradle, Hair-Cutting and the Girl's Three-Day Fast
title.zh: 搖籃、剪髮與少女三日齋

region.zh: 庫斯科家戶(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The life-cycle rites of Molina's account: at conception (ayuscay) the baby was placed on the fourth day in a cradle called quirau before the assembled uncles; at one year came the rutuchico, when the eldest uncle cut the first hair and each relation followed, and the child received the name it was to bear until of age; and at puberty came the quicuchicu for girls, who fasted two days without food, were given a little raw maize on the third lest they die of hunger, were washed and dressed in ancalluasu clothes with white-wool shoes, set food before the principal relations, and received from the principal relation the name she was to bear until death, together with instruction how to behave and obey her parents. This custom was ordained by Inca Yupanqui.
summary.zh: 莫利納所記生命禮俗:懷孕時行「阿尤斯卡伊」,嬰兒於第四日入「基勞」搖籃,請叔伯親友相看;周歲行「魯圖奇科」,由最長的叔伯剪第一縷胎髮,親友依次剪之,並賜名至成年;及笄行「基庫奇庫」,少女前兩日絕食,第三日僅得少許生玉米以免餓斃,第四日沐浴,著白毛鞋與「安卡利亞蘇」衣,梳辮覆囊,向尊長奉食進酒,由至親賜予終身之名,並教以為人處世、孝順父母之道。此俗乃印加·尤潘琪所定。

sensitivity.note: Life-cycle rites from Molina; his remark that the gifts were given 'without any idolatrous practice whatever' is a missionary observation preserved.

passages.text: The ayuscay was when a woman conceived. On the fourth day they put the babies into a cradle called quirau, and they invited the uncles and other relations to see it; but no other ceremony of any kind was performed in consequence of this event.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, life-cycle rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The rutuchico is when the child attains the age of one year. Then, whether it be a boy or a girl, they give it the name that it is to have until it is of age. The child was then shorn, and to perform the ceremony the eldest uncle was called, who cut the first hair. Then the other relations did the same, and afterwards the friends of the parents. They all drank, and the principal uncle gave the child the name it was to bear until it came of age.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, life-cycle rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The quicuchica is when girls reach the age of puberty: they fasted during the two first days, without eating anything at all, and on the third day they were given a little raw maize, that they might not die of hunger. They were confined in a place within the house, and on the fourth day they were washed, and dressed in clothes called ancalluasu, with shoes of white wool. Their hair was plaited, and a sort of bag was placed on their heads. On this day the principal relations came, and the girl came forth to set food before them and to give them to drink. The principal relation gave her the name she was to bear from thenceforth, and taught her how she should behave and obey her parents; and this custom was ordained by Ynca Yupanqui.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, life-cycle rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Marriage by the Inca's Gift: Serving in the Father-in-law's House
title.zh: 印加賜婚:婿入岳家服役

region.zh: 庫斯科及各行省(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: When the Inca gave women as wives they were received because it was the command of the Inca. The man went to the house of the girl's father, not to say that the Inca had given her, but that he desired to serve for her; the relations of the girl were assembled and their consent obtained. The youth remained in the house of his father- and mother-in-law for four or five days, carrying in fuel and straw for them. Thus the agreement was made, and he took the girl for his wife; and because the Inca had given her, it was considered that she was taken until death, and she was received on this understanding, and never deserted.
summary.zh: 印加賜婚之婦,因其為王命而受。男子往女子父親家中,不言印加已賜其女,只說欲為其服役;於是聚集女家親屬,取得同意。婿在岳父母家中留宿四五日,為其運薪搬草。婚約既成,遂娶其女;因是印加所賜,故視為終身之約,依此受之,永不離棄。

sensitivity.note: Marriage custom; tagged divine-marriage loosely as marriage-by-divine-right (the Inca as solar appointor) - interpretive.

passages.text: When the Ynca gave women as wives, they were received because it was the command of the Ynca. The man went to the house of the girl's father, not to say that the Ynca had given her, but that he desired to serve for her, and so the relations of the girl were assembled, and their consent was obtained.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, marriage custom (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The youth remained in the house of his father and mother-in-law for a space of four or five days, and carried in fuel and straw for them. Thus the agreement was made, and he took the girl for his wife; and because the Ynca had given her, it was considered that she was taken until death, and she was received on this understanding, and never deserted.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, marriage custom (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Ccapac-cocha: The Children Sent to Every Huaca of the Empire
title.zh: 卡帕克-科查:獻往全境瓦卡的孩童

region.en: Cuzco and the four suyus, to the empire's extremities (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科與四蘇尤至帝國極境(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Ccapac-cocha, instituted by Pachacutec Ynca Yupanqui, was offered when a new Inca began to reign, that the huacas might give him health and preserve his dominions in peace. From every lineage or tribe of the four suyus one or two children of about ten years were brought to Cuzco with cloth, flocks, gold and silver. The children walked twice round the statues of the Creator, the Sun, the Thunder and the Moon; the sacrifices were divided in four for the four provinces; then the children were strangled - first given to eat and drink that they might not enter the presence of the Creator discontented and hungry - and buried with silver figures of sheep and gold and silver figures of men. Some hearts were torn out yet palpitating and offered to the huacas; the huaca was anointed with blood from ear to ear, which they called pirac. The offerings were relayed across the whole empire by quipu-keepers (the Vilca-camayocs, each charged with nearly five hundred leagues of huaca accounts); if a hill was too steep to climb, the sacrifices were hurled to its summit from slings; no huaca - tree, fountain, hill or lake - was left out, for it was feared the omitted would be enraged and punish the Inca. Bearers of the Ccapac-cocha passed villages in such veneration that the inhabitants stayed within their houses prostrate until they had passed.
summary.zh: 「卡帕克-科查」由帕查庫特克·尤潘琪所立,新王即位時獻祭,求瓦卡賜其安康、保其疆土太平。四蘇尤各族各送一二名約十歲孩童至庫斯科,隨行有布帛、畜群、金銀。孩童繞行造物主、太陽、雷、月神像兩匝;祭品分作四份,以應四省。孩童先予飲食,免其飢餓不滿而入造物主之前,隨後被勒斃,與銀羊、金銀人像一同下葬;有的活剖其心,獻於尚在搏動之際;以血自耳至耳塗抹瓦卡,謂之「皮拉克」。祭品由「維爾卡-卡馬約克」(每人掌管近五百萊格內瓦卡清單的結繩會計)接力送往全境;山勢過陡者,以吊索將祭品拋上峰頂。任何瓦卡——樹、泉、山、湖——皆不得遺漏,否則恐其震怒降罰於印加。抬祭者所過之村,村民深居俯首,待其過後方起。

sensitivity.note: The Capacocha rite is among the best-attested Inca ceremonies (mountain-pl burials corroborate it). Described soberly as an archival record; not romanticized.

passages.text: The Ccapac-cocha was instituted by Pachacutec Ynca Yupanqui. The provinces of Colla-suyu, Chincha-suyu, Anti-suyu, and Cunti-suyu brought to this city, from each lineage or tribe, one or two male and female children aged about ten years. They also brought cloth and flocks, gold and silver. Then the Ynca seated himself in the Huacay-pata, the great square of Cuzco. The children and the other sacrifices walked round the statues of the Creator, the Sun, the Thunder, and the Moon, which were placed in the square, taking two turns. The Ynca then commanded the Priests of the provinces to divide the sacrifices into four parts, in token of the four provinces.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac-cocha (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Lord Ynca offered these sacrifices when he began to reign, that the huacas might give him health and preserve his dominions in peace. No huaca or place of worship, how small soever, was left out in the distribution of the sacrifices. The reason why all the huacas - whether sacred trees, fountains, hills or lakes - received part of the sacrifice was because it was held to be an evil omen if any were left out, and because it was feared that if any were omitted they would be enraged, and would punish the Ynca. If any of the hills were very steep and could not be ascended, the sacrifices were hurled to the summits from slings.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac-cocha (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The first was offered to the Creator. After this prayer they strangled the children, first giving them to eat and drink, that they might not enter the presence of the Creator discontented and hungry. From others they took out the hearts while yet alive, and offered them to the huacas while yet palpitating. They anointed the huaca with the blood from ear to ear, and they called this pirac. For this service the Ynca had Indians in Cuzco who were natives of the four Suyus; each one had a knowledge of all the huacas in the province over which he was Quipucamayoc or Accountant. They were called Vilca-camayoc; each Indian had charge of nearly five hundred leagues of country, and had an account of the things to be sacrificed at every huaca within his district.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac-cocha (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They held this sacrifice, called Ccapacocha or Cachahuaca, in such veneration that, when those who were making journeys over uninhabited tracts with the sacrifices met other travellers, they did not raise their eyes to look at them, and the travellers prostrated themselves on the ground until the sacrifice-bearers had passed. When those bearing sacrifices passed through a village, the inhabitants did not come out of their houses, but remained, with deep humility and reverence, until the said Ccapac-cocha had passed onwards. It was also their custom that, whenever they conquered and subjugated any nations, of selecting some of the handsomest of the conquered people and sending them to Cuzco, where they were sacrificed to the Sun who, as they said, had given them the victory.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac-cocha (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Resurrection of the Huacas: The Seven-Year Apostasy
title.zh: 瓦卡復活:七年背教之亂

region.en: Parinacochas and the provinces of the Viceroyalty (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕里納科查斯及各省(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Apostasy recorded from c. 1560, reported by Luis de Olivera; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: From about 1560 the Indians of Parinacochas, Cuzco, Guamanga, La Paz and even Lima and Arequipa fell into a great apostasy, believing that the huacas which the Christians had burnt and destroyed had been brought to life again, divided into two parts - one united with the huaca Pachacama, the other with the huaca Titicaca - and that they had formed in the air in order of battle against God and conquered Him, killing all the Spaniards and destroying their cities, while the sea would rise to drink them up that they might be remembered no more. The huacas, it was preached, had made the Indians and their land, while God had made only the Spaniards. Preachers declared that the huacas now wandered in the air, thirsty and starving because the Indians no longer sacrificed nor poured out chicha to them, and that fields were sown with worms to be planted in the hearts of Spaniards and of those Indians who remained Christians. The baptized were threatened with death unless they renounced the Christian faith, fasted from salt, aji, coloured maize and all Spanish things, and left their Christian names. Indians possessed by huacas trembled, fell to the ground, and were carried to straw lodgings to be worshipped; a possessed man raised a fragment of a burnt huaca crying 'You see here your support.' The apostasy lasted seven years before priests repressed it.
summary.zh: 約1560年起,帕里納科查斯、庫斯科、關曼加、拉巴斯乃至利馬、阿雷基帕的印第安人陷入大背教:他們相信被基督徒焚毀的瓦卡已經復活,分為兩部分——一合於帕查卡馬克瓦卡,一合於的的喀喀瓦卡——並在空中列陣與上帝作戰而勝之,盡殺西班牙人、毀其城,海水將上漲吞沒一切,使其無人記起。傳道者稱瓦卡造了印第安人與這片土地,上帝只造了西班牙人;瓦卡如今在空中游蕩,飢渴難忍,因為印第安人不再獻祭、不再傾灑奇恰酒;田間播下蠕蟲,將植入西班牙人與仍信基督的印第安人的心中。受洗者若不棄絕信仰、不戒鹽與辣椒與西班牙之物、不改回舊名,便遭殺戮。被瓦卡附體的印第安人顫慄倒地,被抬往草棚受拜;附體者高舉瓦卡殘石呼曰:「看啊,這就是你們的依靠。」背教持續七年,方由教士鎮壓平息。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-period syncretic revival movement, recorded by the persecuting side; tagged resurrection for the huacas-risen belief, a rare post-conquest myth in the making.

passages.text: In the province of Parinacochas, in the diocese of Cuzco, the priest Luis de Olivera learnt that not only in that province, but in all the other provinces and cities of Chuquisaca, La Paz, Cuzco, Guamanga, and even Lima and Arequipa, most of the Indians had fallen into the greatest apostasy, departing from the Catholic Faith and returning to the idolatries which they practised in the time of their infidelity.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, apostasy report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The deception by which these poor people were deceived was the belief that all the huacas which the Christians had burnt and destroyed had been brought to life again; and that they had been divided into two parts, one of which was united with the huaca Pachacama, and the other with the huaca Titicaca. The story went on that they had formed in the air, in order of battle, against God, and that they had conquered Him. It was believed that God and the Spaniards were conquered, all the Spaniards killed, and their cities destroyed, and that the sea would rise to drink them up, that they might be remembered no more. In this apostasy they believed that God our Lord had made the Spaniards, and Castille, and the animals and provisions of Castille; but that the huacas had made the Indians, and this land, and all the things they possessed before the Spaniards came.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, apostasy report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Many preachers went forth from among the Indians, who preached as well in the desert places as in the villages, declaring the resurrection of the huacas, and saying that they now wandered in the air, thirsty and dying of hunger, because the Indians no longer sacrificed nor poured out chicha to them. They declared that many fields were sown with worms, to be planted in the hearts of the Spaniards, and of the Spanish sheep, and of the horses, and also in the hearts of those Indians who remained Christians. Those who would return to the love of the huacas and live were to fast for some days, not eating salt nor aji, nor coloured maize, nor any Spanish thing, nor entering churches, nor using their christian names.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, apostasy report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Many Indians trembled and fell to the ground, and others tore themselves as if they were possessed; and when they presently became quiet, they said that such and such a huaca had entered into their bodies. Then the people took such an one in their arms and carried him to a chosen spot, and there they made a lodging with straw and cloaks, and began to worship the huaca, offering sheep, colla-chicha, llipta, mollo, and other things. Then the possessed shouted and invoked the huaca, and rose up with the fragment of a burnt huaca in his hands, thus addressing the people: 'You see here your support. You see here that which can give you health, and children, and food. Put it in its place, where it was in the days of the Yncas.' At last the apostasy began to wane, but altogether it lasted for seven years.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, apostasy report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Cure at the Meeting of Two Rivers: Colli-sara and Hichoco
title.zh: 雙河匯流處的療疾:科利-薩拉與伊喬科

region.en: Confluence of two rivers, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近雙河匯流處(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: When an Indian fell sick the witches were called to cure him and say whether he would live or die. They ordered him to collect white maize called colli sara, red and yellow cuma-sara, yellow paro-sara, and sea shells of all colours called ymaymana mullu; the wizard ground the maize with the shell and the sick man, breathing on it, offered it to the huacas and vilcas with the words: 'O all the huacas and vilcas of the four provinces of the land, my grandfathers and ancestors, receive this sacrifice, wheresoever you may be, and give me health.' He breathed on coca and offered it to the Sun, Moon and Stars; with a little gold and silver he sacrificed to the Creator; he gave food to the dead on their tombs, pouring out chicha - for the wizard gave him to understand that he was visited with this sickness because the dead were starving. If he could walk to the junction of two rivers, the wizard made him go there and wash his body with water and flour of white maize, saying that he would there leave his illness; and at the end of the ceremony he must confess all his sins, without concealing any: this they called hichoco.
summary.zh: 印第安人患病,便請巫醫診視生死。巫醫命其備白色玉米「科利-薩拉」、紅黃玉米「庫馬-薩拉」、黃玉米「帕羅-薩拉」,以及各色海貝「伊馬伊馬納-穆盧」。巫醫以貝磨玉米,病者對之吹氣,獻於瓦卡與維爾卡,禱曰:「四省一切瓦卡與維爾卡,我的祖父們、先人們,無論你們身在何處,請領受此祭,賜我康健。」再對古柯吹氣,獻於日、月、星辰;以小金銀祭造物主;在墳墓上供食灑酒——因巫醫使他明白:此病乃因死者飢餓所致。若能步行至雙河匯流處,巫醫便命他前往,以水與白玉米粉洗身,說病將留在那裡。禮成之末,還須盡懺己罪、毫不隱瞞——此謂「伊喬科」。

sensitivity.note: Healing rite described from the missionary side; the ancestral invocation shows the huacas as lineage ancestors.

passages.text: When any Indian is sick, these witches are called in to cure him, and to say whether he will live or die. Having pronounced upon the case, they order the sick man to take white maize called colli sara, red and yellow maize called cuma-sara, yellow maize called paro-sara, sea shells called mullu mullu, of all the colours they can collect, which they call ymaymana mullu. When these things are collected, the wizard grinds the maize with the shell, and gives it ground to the sick man that, breathing on it, he may offer it to the huacas and vilcas, with these words: 'O all the huacas and vilcas of the four provinces of the land, my grandfathers and ancestors, receive this sacrifice, wheresoever you may be, and give me health.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, curing rite (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They also make him breathe on a little coca, and offer it to the Sun, praying for health; and the same to the Moon and Stars. Then, with a little gold and silver of little value in his hand, the sick man offers sacrifice to the Creator. Then the wizard commands him to give food to the dead, placing it on their tombs, and pouring out chicha; for the wizard gives the patient to understand that he is visited with this sickness because the dead are starving.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, curing rite (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: If he is able to go on foot to some junction of two rivers, the wizard makes him go there and wash his body with water and flour of white maize, saying that he will there leave his illness. At the end of this ceremony the wizard tells him that, if he would free himself from his sickness, he must confess all his sins, without concealing any. They call this hichoco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, curing rite (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Whatever Excels Is Huaca: Summits, Beauty and the Rest-Stop Gods
title.zh: 凡卓越者皆為瓦卡:峰頂、至美與歇腳之神

region.en: Mountain passes of the Andes (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 安第斯山口(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: It was the custom that, whenever anything excelled all the rest of its kind in beauty, they worshipped it and made it huaca or sacred. They worshipped the summits of all peaks and mountain passes, and offered maize and other things; for they said that, when they ascended any pass and reached the top, they could there rest from the labour of the ascent. This they called chupasitas.
summary.zh: 凡某物在其類中至美超群,人們便崇拜之,奉為瓦卡或神物。一切峰頂與山口皆受崇拜,人們獻上玉米等物;因為他們說,攀登至口,得至其巔,便可歇息勞乏。此謂「丘帕西塔斯」。

sensitivity.note: A concise statement of the Andean logic of sacredness - excellence in kind marks the huaca.

passages.text: It was also their custom that, whenever anything excelled all the rest of its kind in beauty, they worshipped it, and made it huaca or sacred.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They worshipped the summits of all peaks and mountain passes, and offered maize and other things; for they said that, when they ascended any pass and reached the top, they could there rest from the labour of the ascent. This they called chupasitas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
